Impact of U.S. import controls on endangered species in other countries will depend upon two factors: (1) the extent to which the reduction in the U.S. demand is replaced by increased demand elsewhere in nations without import restrictions, and (2) whether removal of those animals from the wild is governed entirely by demand for it as a trade item or whether, as in the case of depredating leopards, those animals are killed for other than trade reasons. Nevertheless, the overall impact of import restrictions will be greater survival of endangered animals in habitats of the world.
An impact on endangered species and subspecies in other countries will occur as a result of technical assistance and wildlife training the Secretary is encouraged and authorized to give foreign countries. The animal impact will be in the form of increased survival of endangered animals in their native habitats. The degree of impact, however, will vary greatly based upon the receptivity of those nations which harbor species endangered worldwide to U.S. assistance.
Implementation of the recently concluded Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora will, of course, be a more effective means of controlling world trade in endangered species than by U.S. law alone. Neither action, however, will directly benefit species which do not figure in trade. Those non-commercial species will be helped only by protection and management of the native habitat. It is encouraging to note that more nations are taking active interest in endangered species preservation.
In the United States, endangered species management programs can be more effectively conceived and carried out by State and Federal Governments.
